vintage: Compiled 2026-10-01 from research/history.json, ownership.json, spending.json, behavior.json (all post-critique) and the GitHub mirrors they cite. Latest data: CPI Aug 2026; saving rate Aug 2026 (BEA 30-Sep-2026 annual update for 2022-2025); labor Aug 2026; Treasury and mortgage rates 10 Sep 2026; Case-Shiller Jul 2026; DFA 2026:Q2; Census income 2025 (P60-289, Sept 2026); population Census Vintage 2025. National-accounts DPI levels are the pre-update vintage.
sources: BLS: CPI-U (datasets/cpi-us), CPS labor force (LNS11300001/2, LNS11300060, Table A-1), CPS union membership and self-employment (US-chartbook), Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024

BEA NIPA Tables 2.1 / 2.6 (personal income, DPI, saving; FRED PSAVERT, DSPI) and the BEA 30-Sep-2026 annual update (Survey of Current Business, Sept 2026, Table 7) for saving rates 2022-2025; BEA Distribution of Personal Income

Federal Reserve: Z.1 Financial Accounts (CMDEBT, HHMSDODNS), G.19 consumer credit, Distributional Financial Accounts (wealth shares), Survey of Consumer Finances 2022, Freddie Mac PMMS (FRED MORTGAGE30US)

Census Bureau: CPS ASEC income (Tables H-8, F-7, P-38/A-7, P60-289), Housing Vacancy Survey, new residential sales (MSPUS), households (TTLHH, HH-6), population estimates Vintage 2025, decennial housing tables, poverty thresholds
S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller US National home price index; R. Shiller monthly S&P composite, dividends and long rate (datasets/s-and-p-500); US Treasury yield curve
WID.world distributional national accounts (Piketty, Saez, Zucman): pre-tax income and net personal wealth shares
NCHS/CDC life expectancy; UN World Population Prospects 2024 (population, fertility)
Social Security Administration: average retired-worker benefit, national average wage index (recalled)
NORC General Social Survey 1972-2024 cumulative file (gssr): respondent earnings and self-employment

Recalled published values (marked basis "recalled" per series): S&P Dow Jones Indices S&P 500 total returns, Census FTYR earnings, FHLBB mortgage rates, Fed G.19 credit-card rates, SSA benefits and AWI, poverty thresholds, CBO and ITEP tax rates

Mirrors: github.com/bdecon/US-chartbook, fartbagxp/economics, rjgreenresearch/economic-fragility-simulator, johnkearns617/AEIEconDataRelease, datasets/*, devxpy/wid_income_chart, PPgp/wpp2024, kjhealy/gssr and others named in each series
note: Household time series for EconomicLives calibration. x is a calendar year unless the unit says otherwise (ageEarnings*, netWorthByAge, homeownershipByAge: age; effectiveTaxRate, personalTaxRateCE, transferShareOfIncome, savingRateByPercentile: income percentile). Money is nominal US dollars of the year; deflate with cpi. YearSeries interpolates between points and holds the end values, so sparse series (every 5 years) are fine for slow-moving quantities. "basis" says whether a series is github-data (official data from a mirror), recalled (published values from memory, marked), or derived (computed here; the note says how).
corrections: savingRate 2022-2025 = BEA post-30-Sep-2026 annual update (3.5 / 6.1 / 6.3 / 5.4), 2026 = Aug 2026 4.1 (research critique section 2); the pre-update 3.0% July 2026 figure is not used.
households: Fed DFA 135.1M (2026:Q1) is canonical for wealth groups (critique section 1); the chained CPS/HVS series ends at 135.4M in 2026, consistent with it.
population: Census Vintage 2025 basis with populationWPP alongside, because UN WPP runs 1.6-2.4% higher in 2020-2026 (critique section 3.6).
effectiveTaxRate is flagged low-confidence (critique section 3.4: CBO distribution figures are recalled).
medianHouseholdIncome 2024 = revised $83,160 (Sept-2026 Census release), not the first-published $83,730.

cpi.unit: index, 1982-84 = 100 (CPI-U, US city average, all items, NSA; annual average of monthly values)
cpi.note: Annual average of monthly index values. 2025 averages 11 months (the October 2025 CPI was never collected because of the federal shutdown); 2026 = January-August average (partial year). 1950-2026 reproduce the research table exactly; 1946-1949 come from the same monthly file. To express a nominal amount of year y in 2025 dollars multiply by cpi(2025) / cpi(y) = 321.943 / cpi(y).

savingRate.unit: % of disposable personal income (personal saving / DPI)
savingRate.source: BEA NIPA Table 2.1: 1947-1958 from the quarterly table in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jannib69/Bitcoin_Prediction_TFT_LSTM_GRU (BEA T20100, older vintage); 1959-2021 FRED PSAVERT annual averages (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fartbagxp/economics/main/data/raw/psavert.csv); 2022-2025 BEA 30-Sep-2026 annual update (SCB Sept 2026 Table 7, research critique); 2026 = August 2026 (post-update).
savingRate.note: DATA-EDITOR CORRECTION APPLIED: 2022-2025 use the post-30-Sep-2026 annual rates 3.5 / 6.1 / 6.3 / 5.4 (pre-update values were 3.35 / 5.59 / 5.43 / 4.58, still used by circuit.json personalHistory, whose income levels are pre-update). 2026 is the single month of August 2026 (4.1%, post-update); the pre-update "3.0% in July 2026" is superseded. 1947-1958 are annual saving / annual DPI from the older-vintage quarterly table (its 1959-1962 values agree with PSAVERT within 0.01 pp). Years 1959-2021 are averages of monthly rates from the pre-update vintage; treat the saving leg as +/-0.8 pp.

householdDebtToIncome.unit: % of disposable personal income (household debt outstanding at year end / annual DPI)
householdDebtToIncome.source: Fed Z.1 households & nonprofits debt securities and loans (CMDEBT, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/miguel-merlin/ebm_foward_returns_forecaster mirror, 1970-2025Q3); before 1970 Z.1 home mortgages (HHMSDODNS) + G.19 consumer credit (TOTALSL); DPI = BEA annual average (FRED DSPI from 1959, BEA T2.1 before); 2026 = derived from the US-chartbook Z.1-based ratio change to 2026:Q2. Research history.json householdDebt_1950_2026.
householdDebtToIncome.note: Debt at Q4 (2025 = Q3, latest in the mirror) over the annual-average DPI of the same year; reproduces every research row within 0.1 pp. Before 1970 the numerator is mortgages + consumer credit only (other household debt was small). Peak 136% in 2007 (Q4 debt / 2007 DPI; 129% in 2005); 2025 = 90.5%. 2026 = 90.0% DERIVED (2026:Q2 debt / Jan-Jul DPI): the 2025 level x the US-chartbook ratio change from 2025 to 2026:Q2 (93.0% -> 92.5%; the chartbook times DPI differently and runs ~2.5 pp above this series in 2025, so its level is not spliced in). Mortgages + consumer credit growth to 2026:Q2 applied to CMDEBT gives the same ~89.9%. DPI is the pre-Sept-2026 vintage (post-update DPI levels were not obtainable), so ratios for 2022-2025 may move by ~1 pp.

consumerCreditToIncome.unit: % of disposable personal income (consumer credit outstanding in December / annual DPI)
consumerCreditToIncome.source: Fed G.19 total consumer credit (TOTALSL, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rjgreenresearch/economic-fragility-simulator mirror; Jul-2026 = revolving + nonrevolving, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fartbagxp/economics); DPI as for householdDebtToIncome.
consumerCreditToIncome.note: Consumer credit = credit cards and other revolving credit + auto, student and other nonrevolving loans (not mortgages). Revolving (card) credit alone was 0.7% of DPI in 1970, 9.2% in 2000 and 5.8% in 2025 (research householdDebt_1950_2026). 2026 = July 2026 stock / Jan-Jul DPI. Pre-update DPI vintage.

homeownership.unit: % of occupied housing units that are owner-occupied
homeownership.source: Census decennial census (1940-1960, recalled) and CPS/Housing Vacancy Survey (1965-2026, annual average of quarterly NSA rates; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/haydn-s/sourcing-data-project-1 FRED RHORUSQ156N mirror). Research history.json.
homeownership.note: 1940, 1950 and 1960 are decennial-census values (recalled; decennial levels run ~1 pp below the HVS in overlapping years, e.g. 1970 62.9 vs 64.2). 2026 = Q1-Q2 average. The 1940 point is kept so that 1946-1949 interpolate between censuses.

housePriceIndex.unit: index, 2025 = 100 (nominal US national home prices, annual average)
housePriceIndex.source: S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller US National index (NSA, monthly; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasets/house-prices-us national-month.csv, 1975-Jul 2026); before 1975 Census/HUD median new-house sales price (MSPUS, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobgdickson/builder-regulator-balance) and decennial-census median home values (recalled). Research history.json housePrices_1940_2026.
housePriceIndex.note: Annual average of the monthly national index, rebased so 2025 = 100 (2025 average 328.51 on the Jan-2000 = 100 base). 2026 = Jan-Jul. S&P publishes the national index from 1987; the 1975-1986 values in the mirror are the spliced Shiller back-series. DERIVED SPLICE: 1963-1974 move with MSPUS (new homes, not quality-adjusted) and 1950 / 1960 with the decennial median value of owner-occupied homes relative to 1970 ($7,354 / $11,900 / $17,000), so the pre-1975 part is approximate (+/-10%) and overstates pure price growth slightly (homes got bigger). Real prices: divide by cpi.

medianHomePrice.unit: $ nominal (median sales price of new houses sold, annual)
medianHomePrice.source: Census/HUD median sales price of new houses sold (MSPUS quarterly 1963-2024, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobgdickson/builder-regulator-balance; 2025-2026 averages of monthly new-home medians, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/nhs_p.csv); 1950/1960 derived from decennial-census median home values (recalled). Research history.json housePrices_1940_2026.
medianHomePrice.note: NEW homes, which are larger and dearer than the existing stock (NAR's 2025 existing-home median, ~$410K recalled, is close, but in earlier decades new homes ran ~40% above the census median value). 1950 and 1960 = census median value of owner-occupied homes x 1.38, the MSPUS / census-value ratio of 1970, 1980 and 2000 (1.38, 1.37, 1.40); derived, +/-15%. 2026 = Jan-Jul. Price-to-median-household-income: 2.7 (1970), 4.0 (2000), 5.8 (2022), 4.7 (2025).

equityTotalReturn.unit: % per calendar year (S&P 500 price change + reinvested dividends, nominal; 2026 = Jan-Sep, not annualized)
equityTotalReturn.source: recalled: S&P Dow Jones Indices' published S&P 500 annual total returns (the standard table, as reproduced e.g. by slickcharts.com; A. Damodaran's index-plus-dividend table and Ibbotson SBBI differ from it by up to ~0.5 pp in some years); checked against Shiller monthly S&P composite price and dividends (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasets/s-and-p-500 data.csv, research history.json stockMarket_1950_2026).
equityTotalReturn.note: Calendar-year (Dec-close to Dec-close) total returns. VERIFIED against the Shiller data in the research mirror: over 1950-2022 (73 years) the recalled values correlate 0.988 with total returns computed from Shiller December monthly averages, with geometric means 11.24% vs 11.21% per year; the mean absolute gap (2.0 pp) comes from monthly averaging (largest 1991/1992, when the Dec-1990 average sat well below the year-end close). 2025 = 17.88 (price return 16.4% + dividends). 2026 = DERIVED partial year: Shiller September-2026 average / December-2025 average (+11.9%) plus 3/4 of the 1.1% dividend yield. Real return = (1 + r) x cpi(y-1) / cpi(y) - 1.

treasury10y.unit: % per year (10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield, annual average)
treasury10y.source: Shiller "Long Interest Rate" (= FRED GS10 monthly from 1953; long-term government bond yield before), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasets/s-and-p-500 data.csv, 1946-2022; US Treasury daily par yield curve via https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/treas_raw.csv, 2023-2026.
treasury10y.note: Annual averages. The two sources agree within 0.03 pp in every overlapping year 1988-2022. 2026 = 1 Jan - 10 Sep (daily); the 10-year was 4.95% on 10 Sep 2026 (the research critique cites ~5.3% on 30 Sep 2026, not in the mirror). Before 1953 the series is a long-term (10+ year) government bond yield.

mortgageRate30y.unit: % per year (30-year fixed-rate mortgage, annual average)
mortgageRate30y.source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey (MORTGAGE30US weekly, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rjgreenresearch/economic-fragility-simulator mirror to Apr 2026 + https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/mortgage.csv to 10 Sep 2026), 1971-2026; recalled: FHLBB contract rate on conventional new-home mortgages (FRED MORTG), 1963-1970; derived before 1963.
mortgageRate30y.note: Annual averages of weekly rates (2026 = Jan-10 Sep; 6.76% on 10 Sep 2026). 1963-1970 = FHLBB average contract rate on conventional loans for new homes (recalled, +/-0.15 pp; a different survey from PMMS). 1950-1962 DERIVED = 10-year Treasury + 1.69 pp (the 1963-1965 FHLBB-minus-10y spread); FHA-insured loans then carried a 4.25-5.25% ceiling and conventional loans ~4.5-6%, so treat 1950s values as +/-0.5 pp. Rates were fixed for the life of the loan, so a household keeps its purchase-year rate.

creditCardApr.unit: % per year (average interest rate on credit-card plans, all accounts; approximate before 1972)
creditCardApr.source: recalled: Federal Reserve G.19 "Commercial bank interest rate on credit card plans, all accounts" (FRED TERMCBCCALLNS, from 1994; the older G.19 credit-card plan rate from 1972), annual averages of the published months; before 1972 approximate.
creditCardApr.note: APPROXIMATE (+/-1 pp; no credit-card rate series is in the research mirrors). 1950-1970 = 18%, the usual 1.5% per month on department-store revolving accounts and the first bank cards (BankAmericard 1958), capped by state usury laws until the 1978 Marquette decision. Accounts actually assessed interest pay ~1.5-2 pp more (~22-23% in 2024-2025; research spending.json uses ~22% and an ~18% effective yield on all balances). Use for the cost of revolving debt (jeopardy) in the year it is carried.

lfprMale.unit: % of the civilian noninstitutional male population age 16+ in the labor force (annual average)
lfprMale.source: BLS CPS LNS11300001 (monthly SA), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fartbagxp/economics/main/data/raw/lns11300001.csv. Research history.json laborForceParticipation_1950_2026.
lfprMale.note: Annual average of monthly rates, 1948-2026 (2025 = 11 months, no October 2025 survey; 2026 = Jan-Aug). 86.3% in 1950 -> 67.1% in 2026: longer schooling, earlier retirement, disability and an older population. Prime-age (25-54) men: 96.5% (1950) -> 89.2% (2025), research (recalled).

lfprFemale.unit: % of the civilian noninstitutional female population age 16+ in the labor force (annual average)
lfprFemale.source: BLS CPS LNS11300002 (monthly SA), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fartbagxp/economics/main/data/raw/lns11300002.csv. Research history.json.
lfprFemale.note: Annual average of monthly rates, 1948-2026 (2025 = 11 months; 2026 = Jan-Aug). 33.9% in 1950, peak 60.0% in 1999-2000, 56.9% in 2026. Prime-age (25-54) women: 36.8% (1950) -> 77.8% (2025), research (recalled).

unemployment.unit: % of the civilian labor force (annual average)
unemployment.source: BLS CPS Table A-1 annual averages 1946-2025 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasets/employment-us aat1.csv, research history.json employmentCPS_1950_2025); 2026 = Jan-Aug from CPS microdata counts (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/cps_lfs.csv).
unemployment.note: 2026 is unemployed / (employed + unemployed) averaged over Jan-Aug 2026 from the US-chartbook microdata series; the same calculation reproduces the official annual rate within 0.05 pp in 2019-2025. 1947 uses the 16+ basis (the file also has a 14+ row). Peaks: 9.7% (1982), 9.6% (2010), 8.1% (2020).

employmentRate25to54Male.unit: % of men age 25-54 who are employed
employmentRate25to54Male.source: derived from research history.json laborForceParticipation_1950_2026 (men25to54_recalled) and unemployment
employmentRate25to54Male.note: DERIVED: prime-age LFPR by sex (research history.json, recalled from BLS LNS11300061/62, +/-0.5 pp) x (1 - prime-age unemployment), where prime-age unemployment = 0.83 x the overall rate (mean ratio over 1989-2025 of 1 - EPOP/LFPR for ages 25-54, both sexes, from CPS microdata [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/epop.csv] and BLS LNS11300060, to the overall annual rate; range 0.76-0.91). Same factor for both sexes (men run ~0.3 pp higher in recessions). Uncertainty ~ +/-1 pp. Points every 5 years 1950-2015 and annually 2019-2025. Prime-age men: ~93% employed in the 1950s-60s, 86-87% since 2023.

employmentRate25to54Female.unit: % of women age 25-54 who are employed
employmentRate25to54Female.source: derived from research history.json laborForceParticipation_1950_2026 (women25to54_recalled) and unemployment
employmentRate25to54Female.note: DERIVED: prime-age LFPR by sex (research history.json, recalled from BLS LNS11300061/62, +/-0.5 pp) x (1 - prime-age unemployment), where prime-age unemployment = 0.83 x the overall rate (mean ratio over 1989-2025 of 1 - EPOP/LFPR for ages 25-54, both sexes, from CPS microdata [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/epop.csv] and BLS LNS11300060, to the overall annual rate; range 0.76-0.91). Same factor for both sexes (men run ~0.3 pp higher in recessions). Uncertainty ~ +/-1 pp. Points every 5 years 1950-2015 and annually 2019-2025. Prime-age women: ~35% employed in 1950, ~75% since 2023.

selfEmploymentRate.unit: % of employed people who are self-employed (unincorporated + incorporated)
selfEmploymentRate.source: BLS CPS self-employment (unincorporated + incorporated, % of labor force; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/selfemp.csv, research behavior.json selfEmployment_CPS) 1989-2026; GSS wrkslf among workers (research behavior.json gssWorkAttitudes) 1972-1988; derived from CPS agricultural employment (aat1) 1950-1970.
selfEmploymentRate.note: 1989-2026: BLS share of the labor force / (1 - unemployment rate) -> share of the employed (2026 = Jan-Aug). 1972-1988 DERIVED: GSS self-employed share of workers, 5-survey moving average, scaled by 0.843 so that GSS matches BLS in 1989-1991 (GSS runs ~2.5 pp above BLS). 1950-1970 DERIVED: the 1974 value + 0.65 x (agricultural share of employment minus its 1974 value), 0.65 being roughly the self-employed + unpaid-family share of farm employment; this captures the collapse of family farming but NOT the decline of nonfarm proprietors (corner shops, independent professionals), so 1950-1965 are likely 2-3 pp too low (true 1950 level probably ~17-18%). The modern rate is ~10% of the employed; owning a business is one of the strongest markers of "a life path you control" in the brief.

unionMembership.unit: % of wage and salary workers who are union members
unionMembership.source: BLS CPS union membership: CPS microdata 12-month averages (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/union.csv) 1989-2026; recalled before 1989 (Mayer 2004, CRS RL32553; BLS). Research history.json unionMembership_1950_2026.
unionMembership.note: Pre-1983 values use nonagricultural employment as the denominator (not strictly comparable; ~1-2 pp higher than a wage-and-salary basis). Peak ~35% in 1954. 1989+ = 12-month average ending December (2026: ending August). Private sector ~6%, public sector ~32% (2024).

earningsMedianMale.unit: $ nominal per year (median annual earnings of all men 15+ with earnings, incl. part-time and part-year)
earningsMedianMale.source: derived from Census FTYR medians (recalled), CPS ASEC 2024 earnings distribution (research) and GSS 1974-2024 microdata (research behavior inputs)
earningsMedianMale.note: DERIVED (no all-worker earnings-by-sex series is in the research): (1) men's FULL-TIME YEAR-ROUND median earnings (Census Historical Income Table P-38 / P60 Table A-7, recalled; see earningsMedianMaleFTYR) x 0.887, the all-worker / FTYR factor fitted so that the 2024 men + women all-worker distribution has the CPS ASEC median of ~$52,000 (US-chartbook pearn_dist.csv from CPS ASEC 2025 microdata, research ownership.json personIncomeDistribution_2024; lognormal earnings with sd 0.85, women 47.6% of earners, both assumptions) and held constant over time; (2) women = men x femaleToMaleEarnings. Uncertainty ~ +/-5% on levels (2024 men 61490, women 43230). 1950 scales 1955 by median family income; 2024-2025 use the Census P60-289 FTYR facts in the research (FTYR median $66,620 in 2025; ratios 0.806 / 0.839). The scene calibrates earnings to BEA wages anyway, so the time path and the sex gap matter more than the level.

earningsMedianFemale.unit: $ nominal per year (median annual earnings of all women 15+ with earnings, incl. part-time and part-year)
earningsMedianFemale.source: derived from Census FTYR medians (recalled), CPS ASEC 2024 earnings distribution (research) and GSS 1974-2024 microdata (research behavior inputs)
earningsMedianFemale.note: DERIVED (no all-worker earnings-by-sex series is in the research): (1) men's FULL-TIME YEAR-ROUND median earnings (Census Historical Income Table P-38 / P60 Table A-7, recalled; see earningsMedianMaleFTYR) x 0.887, the all-worker / FTYR factor fitted so that the 2024 men + women all-worker distribution has the CPS ASEC median of ~$52,000 (US-chartbook pearn_dist.csv from CPS ASEC 2025 microdata, research ownership.json personIncomeDistribution_2024; lognormal earnings with sd 0.85, women 47.6% of earners, both assumptions) and held constant over time; (2) women = men x femaleToMaleEarnings. Uncertainty ~ +/-5% on levels (2024 men 61490, women 43230). 1950 scales 1955 by median family income; 2024-2025 use the Census P60-289 FTYR facts in the research (FTYR median $66,620 in 2025; ratios 0.806 / 0.839). The scene calibrates earnings to BEA wages anyway, so the time path and the sex gap matter more than the level.

femaleToMaleEarnings.unit: ratio (women's / men's median annual earnings, all workers with earnings)
femaleToMaleEarnings.source: derived: Census FTYR female-to-male ratio (recalled; 2024-2025 research) x GSS all-worker / full-time ratio multiplier (GSS 1972-2024 cumulative file, https://github.com/kjhealy/gssr gss_all.rda, respondent earnings conrinc/realrinc, weighted grouped medians)
femaleToMaleEarnings.note: All-worker ratio = official FTYR ratio x m(y), where m = (GSS women/men median among ALL earners) / (GSS women/men median among full-time workers), pooled over survey windows: 1977: 0.808, 1988: 0.874, 1999: 0.922, 2010: 0.896, 2020: 0.872; interpolated, held flat at the ends (1950-1976 held at the first window's value (0.808, centred on 1977), so the 1950s-60s gap may be understated). Women's part-time and part-year work makes the all-worker ratio (0.49 in 1960, 0.70 in 2024, 0.73 in 2025) lower than the FTYR ratio (0.61 in 1960, 0.81-0.84 in 2024-25); see femaleToMaleEarningsFTYR. Equals earningsMedianFemale / earningsMedianMale.

earningsMedianMaleFTYR.unit: $ nominal per year (median earnings of men working full-time, year-round)
earningsMedianMaleFTYR.source: recalled: Census Historical Income Table P-38 / P60 report Table A-7 (FTYR workers 15+ from 1980, 14+ before); 2024-2025 derived from research ownership.json / history.json Census P60-289 facts
earningsMedianMaleFTYR.note: 1955-2023 recalled (+/-2%; the implied ratios match the published 63.9% (1955), 60.7% (1960), 59.4% (1970), 60.2% (1980), 71.6% (1990), 77.4% (2010), 82.7% (2023)). 1950 DERIVED (1955 x median family income 1950/1955). 2025 DERIVED: the both-sexes FTYR median $66,620 = men x ratio^0.44 (women ~44% of FTYR workers; log-mixture approximation) with ratio 0.839 -> men 71970; 2024 = geometric mean of 2023 and 2025 (ratio 0.806 applied to women).

earningsMedianFemaleFTYR.unit: $ nominal per year (median earnings of women working full-time, year-round)
earningsMedianFemaleFTYR.source: recalled: Census Historical Income Table P-38 / P60 report Table A-7; 2024-2025 derived from research Census P60-289 facts

femaleToMaleEarningsFTYR.unit: ratio (women's / men's median earnings, full-time year-round workers)
femaleToMaleEarningsFTYR.source: Census P-38 / Table A-7 (recalled); 2024 = 0.806 and 2025 = 0.839 from research history.json personalIncomeByAgeSex_2024_approx (sibling search-verified, Census P60-289)
femaleToMaleEarningsFTYR.note: The official "cents on the dollar" statistic: 0.64 (1955), ~0.59 in 1970-1975 (the annual low, ~0.57 in 1973, falls between these 5-yearly points), 0.72 (1990), 0.77 (2010), 0.84 (2022), dip to 0.806 in 2024, 0.839 in 2025.

top1IncomeShare.unit: % of pre-tax national income received by the top 1% of adults
top1IncomeShare.source: WID.world sptincj992 p99p100 (https://media.githubusercontent.com/media/devxpy/wid_income_chart/main/wid_all_data/WID_data_US.csv; research history.json topSharesWID_1950_2024)
top1IncomeShare.note: WID.world distributional national accounts (Piketty-Saez-Zucman): share of pre-tax national income held by the group, adults with income split equally between spouses. Annual 1946-2024; WID marks 2023-2024 as nowcasts (2024 = 2023; both within 0.1 pp of 2022), so the series is flat after 2022 and held for 2025-2026. Tax-unit fiscal series (Piketty-Saez, incl. capital gains, research ownership.json topIncomeShares) run higher at the top (top 1% ~22% in TY2022 per IRS SOI via Tax Foundation). 16.4% (1950) -> 10.4% (1970s) -> 20.7% (2022).

top10IncomeShare.unit: % of pre-tax national income received by the top 10% of adults
top10IncomeShare.source: WID.world sptincj992 p90p100 (devxpy/wid_income_chart mirror; research history.json topSharesWID_1950_2024)
top10IncomeShare.note: WID.world distributional national accounts (Piketty-Saez-Zucman): share of pre-tax national income held by the group, adults with income split equally between spouses. Annual 1946-2024; WID marks 2023-2024 as nowcasts (2024 = 2023; both within 0.1 pp of 2022), so the series is flat after 2022 and held for 2025-2026. Tax-unit fiscal series (Piketty-Saez, incl. capital gains, research ownership.json topIncomeShares) run higher at the top (top 1% ~22% in TY2022 per IRS SOI via Tax Foundation). Bottom 50%: 19.0% (1950), 21.1% (1970), 13.3-13.4% (2022-24), see bottom50IncomeShare.

bottom50IncomeShare.unit: % of pre-tax national income received by the bottom 50% of adults
bottom50IncomeShare.note: WID.world distributional national accounts (Piketty-Saez-Zucman): share of pre-tax national income held by the group, adults with income split equally between spouses. Annual 1946-2024; WID marks 2023-2024 as nowcasts (2024 = 2023; both within 0.1 pp of 2022), so the series is flat after 2022 and held for 2025-2026. Tax-unit fiscal series (Piketty-Saez, incl. capital gains, research ownership.json topIncomeShares) run higher at the top (top 1% ~22% in TY2022 per IRS SOI via Tax Foundation).

top1WealthShare.unit: % of household net worth held by the wealthiest 1% of households
top1WealthShare.source: Fed DFA (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fartbagxp/economics/main/data/raw/fed_dfa_wealth_by_percentile.csv; research history.json wealthSharesDFA_1989_2026) and WID.world shwealj992 (devxpy/wid_income_chart mirror) before 1989
top1WealthShare.note: Households' net worth. 1989-2026 = Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts, mean of the quarters of each year (1989: Q3-Q4; 2026: Q1-Q2), from the release that includes 2026:Q2; circuit.json groupHistory used the June-2026 release (detailed levels to 2026:Q1), so the two differ by up to 0.29 pp from revisions. 1950-1988 DERIVED: WID.world net personal wealth shares (equal-split adults, shwealj992) rescaled to the DFA level at 1989 (top 1% x 0.793, top 10% x 0.939; bottom 50% = the spliced bottom 90% x 0.0884, its DFA 1989 share of the bottom 90%, the rule circuit.json uses, because the WID bottom-50 share is near zero and noisy). circuit.json applied the same splice to recalled Saez-Zucman anchors, so pre-1989 top shares differ from it by ~0.5-1.5 pp. Unspliced WID levels (more concentrated: top 1% 34.8-34.9% in 2022-24) are in the *WID series. Record 32.5% in 2026:Q2.

top10WealthShare.unit: % of household net worth held by the wealthiest 10% of households
top10WealthShare.note: Households' net worth. 1989-2026 = Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts, mean of the quarters of each year (1989: Q3-Q4; 2026: Q1-Q2), from the release that includes 2026:Q2; circuit.json groupHistory used the June-2026 release (detailed levels to 2026:Q1), so the two differ by up to 0.29 pp from revisions. 1950-1988 DERIVED: WID.world net personal wealth shares (equal-split adults, shwealj992) rescaled to the DFA level at 1989 (top 1% x 0.793, top 10% x 0.939; bottom 50% = the spliced bottom 90% x 0.0884, its DFA 1989 share of the bottom 90%, the rule circuit.json uses, because the WID bottom-50 share is near zero and noisy). circuit.json applied the same splice to recalled Saez-Zucman anchors, so pre-1989 top shares differ from it by ~0.5-1.5 pp. Unspliced WID levels (more concentrated: top 1% 34.8-34.9% in 2022-24) are in the *WID series.

bottom50WealthShare.unit: % of household net worth held by the least wealthy 50% of households
bottom50WealthShare.note: Households' net worth. 1989-2026 = Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts, mean of the quarters of each year (1989: Q3-Q4; 2026: Q1-Q2), from the release that includes 2026:Q2; circuit.json groupHistory used the June-2026 release (detailed levels to 2026:Q1), so the two differ by up to 0.29 pp from revisions. 1950-1988 DERIVED: WID.world net personal wealth shares (equal-split adults, shwealj992) rescaled to the DFA level at 1989 (top 1% x 0.793, top 10% x 0.939; bottom 50% = the spliced bottom 90% x 0.0884, its DFA 1989 share of the bottom 90%, the rule circuit.json uses, because the WID bottom-50 share is near zero and noisy). circuit.json applied the same splice to recalled Saez-Zucman anchors, so pre-1989 top shares differ from it by ~0.5-1.5 pp. Unspliced WID levels (more concentrated: top 1% 34.8-34.9% in 2022-24) are in the *WID series. DFA low 0.4% in 2010 (negative home equity); 2.3% in 2026.

top1WealthShareWID.unit: % of net personal wealth held by the group of adults (WID.world, equal-split)
top1WealthShareWID.source: WID.world shwealj992 p99p100 (devxpy/wid_income_chart mirror; research history.json topSharesWID_1950_2024)
top1WealthShareWID.note: Unspliced WID level for reference (2023-2024 nowcast; 2024 = 2023, within 0.1 pp of 2022). Adults, equal-split, net personal wealth incl. pensions; more concentrated than the household-based DFA.

top10WealthShareWID.unit: % of net personal wealth held by the group of adults (WID.world, equal-split)
top10WealthShareWID.source: WID.world shwealj992 p90p100 (devxpy/wid_income_chart mirror; research history.json topSharesWID_1950_2024)
top10WealthShareWID.note: Unspliced WID level for reference (2023-2024 nowcast; 2024 = 2023, within 0.1 pp of 2022). Adults, equal-split, net personal wealth incl. pensions; more concentrated than the household-based DFA.

bottom50WealthShareWID.unit: % of net personal wealth held by the group of adults (WID.world, equal-split)
bottom50WealthShareWID.source: WID.world shwealj992 p0p50 (devxpy/wid_income_chart mirror; research history.json topSharesWID_1950_2024)
bottom50WealthShareWID.note: Unspliced WID level for reference (2023-2024 nowcast; 2024 = 2023, within 0.1 pp of 2022). Adults, equal-split, net personal wealth incl. pensions; more concentrated than the household-based DFA.

collegeShare25plus.unit: % of people age 25+ with a bachelor's degree or more (4+ years of college before 1993)
collegeShare25plus.source: Census CPS Historical Table A-2 (recalled, +/-0.3 pp) and CPS microdata 12 months to Aug 2026 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/cps_educ.csv). Research history.json educationalAttainment_1940_2026.
collegeShare25plus.note: 6.2% (1950) -> 25.6% (2000) -> 39.8% (2026). Pre-1993 counts "4 or more years of college". High school or more: 34.3% (1950) -> 92.1% (2026). The research has no value between 1950 and 1960 (the loader interpolates).

socialSecurityAvgBenefit.unit: $ nominal per year (average Social Security retired-worker benefit; December level x 12)
socialSecurityAvgBenefit.source: recalled: SSA Annual Statistical Supplement (average monthly benefit of retired workers in current-payment status, December) and SSA COLA fact sheets (the 2019-2025 points are the average of the following January, after the COLA, e.g. 2025 = January 2026 $2,071); checked against SSA all-beneficiary averages 1988-2026 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/ss_beneficiaries.csv).
socialSecurityAvgBenefit.note: December level of each year (which includes the cost-of-living adjustment paid from January), times 12. CHECK: the ratio of these retired-worker values to the mirror's all-beneficiary December averages is 1990 1.107, 1995 1.109, 2000 1.101, 2005 1.094, 2010 1.094, 2019 1.088, 2020 1.085, a smooth drift, which supports the recalled values. 2015 DERIVED = mirror all-beneficiary Dec-2015 average x 1.091 (interpolated ratio). The 1950 value reflects the 1950 amendments (+77%; Dec 1949 was ~$26). 2025 = $2,071/month (after the 2.8% COLA for 2026).

averageWageIndex.unit: $ nominal per year (SSA national average wage index)
averageWageIndex.source: recalled: Social Security Administration, National Average Wage Index series (1951-2024); 2025 derived
averageWageIndex.note: Average W-2 wages per worker, used by SSA to index career earnings and the benefit formula. 2025 DERIVED = 2024 x BEA wages and salaries growth (12,958.7 / 12,387.9 $B) / CPS employment growth (163.49 / 161.35 M) = 72105 (SSA publishes 2025 in Oct 2026).

socialSecurityReplacement.unit: ratio 0..1 (average retired-worker benefit per year / average wage index of the year)
socialSecurityReplacement.source: derived from socialSecurityAvgBenefit and averageWageIndex (both SSA, recalled)
socialSecurityReplacement.note: A population-level replacement ratio: the average retiree's benefit relative to the average current wage (1950 uses the 1951 wage index). Rose from ~0.19-0.23 in the 1950s-60s to ~0.31-0.35 from 1980 on (low 0.315 in 2000) after the 1972-77 benefit increases. Individual replacement of one's own career-average indexed earnings is higher at the bottom (the benefit formula is progressive: ~75% for low earners, ~40% medium, ~27% high).

povertyLineFamily4.unit: $ nominal per year (official poverty threshold, weighted average for a family of four)
povertyLineFamily4.source: recalled: Census Bureau historical poverty thresholds (weighted average, family of 4), 1959-2023; derived otherwise
povertyLineFamily4.note: The Orshansky threshold (3 x the 1963 economy food budget) indexed by CPI-U; 1959 x CPI(2023)/CPI(1959) reproduces the 2023 value within 0.4%, confirming the recalled levels. DERIVED: 1950 and 1955 back-cast from 1959 by CPI-U (the line did not exist before 1963-69); 2024 and 2025 = 2023 x CPI-U. Official poverty rate 2025: 10.2% (34.5M people, research ownership.json). Compare to median household income: ~0.48 (1967: $3,410 / $7,143) vs 0.38 (2025) - the line is a fixed basket, not a relative standard, so it falls behind median income as real incomes grow.

medianHouseholdIncome.unit: $ nominal per year (Census CPS ASEC money income, median of all households)
medianHouseholdIncome.source: Census Table H-8 via FRED MEHOINUSA646N (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/duncanburns2013-dot/Housing-Affordability-Crisis mirror) 1984-2025; 1967-1983 recalled from Census H-8; 2025 = Census P60-289. Research history.json medianIncomeHistory_1950_2025.
medianHouseholdIncome.note: Pre-tax cash income incl. cash transfers, excl. capital gains and in-kind benefits. 2024 = $83,160 as revised in Sept 2026 (first published $83,730); 2025 = $87,460 (record, +2.6% real). 1967-1983 recalled (verify). 1950-1965 DERIVED = median family income x 0.900 (the 1967 household/family ratio; the household series starts 1967; the ratio was falling ~0.4 pp a year in 1967-70, so 1950s values may be ~2-3% low). CPI-U deflation shows less real growth than Census's official CPI-U-RS series.

medianFamilyIncome.unit: $ nominal per year (Census CPS ASEC money income, median of families of 2+ related people)
medianFamilyIncome.source: Census Table F-7 via FRED MEFAINUSA646N (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/calebleehill1993/personal-development and rafael-curran mirrors) 1953-2024; 1947 and 1950 recalled (Census P-60); 2025 derived. Research history.json medianIncomeHistory_1950_2025.
medianFamilyIncome.note: 1947 ($3,031) and 1950 ($3,319) recalled from Census P-60 historical tables (plausible, unverified per the research critique). 1951-1952 absent (interpolate). 2025 DERIVED = 2024 x median household income growth 2024-25 (+5.2%), because the 2025 family median is not in the research.

meanHouseholdSize.source: recalled: Census Historical Households Table HH-6 (research history.json householdsAndSize_1950_2026)
meanHouseholdSize.note: 3.37 (1950) -> 2.50 (2025); 2021-2025 approximate (+/-0.02). Fewer children, more people living alone (living-alone share of adults roughly tripled since 1950; research behavior.json livingAlone_byAge_IPUMS).

households.source: Census CPS ASEC/HVS total households (FRED TTLHH, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avikd95/US-Home-Prices mirror) 1947-2023; 2024-2026 chained with Census HVS occupied housing units (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/hhform_lvl.csv; research history.json householdsAndSize_1950_2026).
households.note: March CPS counts, annual (1946 absent). 2024-2026 DERIVED = 2023 CPS level x HVS growth since 2023 (HVS levels run ~2-4M lower than CPS in the 2010s-20s, so they are not spliced by level). The result (135.4M in 2026) matches the Fed DFA count of 135.13M households (2026:Q1), the canonical count for wealth groups per the research critique.

population.unit: millions of people (US resident population, 1 July; Census basis)
population.source: Census Bureau national population estimates, Vintage 2025 (monthly, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/pop_est.csv; research history.json populationTotals_2020_2026) 1990-2026; recalled Census July-1 national estimates (Current Population Reports P-25, total incl. armed forces overseas) 1950-1985.
population.note: 1 July of each year (2026 = Census short-term projection). 1950-1985 are recalled Census estimates every 5 years that include armed forces overseas (0.3-1.0M more than the resident population; most in 1970); each is within 2% of UN WPP 2024 (checked). The why-2 population graphs use UN WPP, which runs 1.6-2.4% above Census in 2020-2026 (higher assumed immigration; the Census/WPP ratio was already 0.985 in 1990); per the research critique, rescale WPP pyramids by population / populationWPP.

populationWPP.unit: millions of people (UN World Population Prospects 2024, 1 July, medium variant from 2024)
populationWPP.source: UN WPP 2024 via the wpp2024 R package (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PPgp/wpp2024), research history.json gdp_1950_2026
populationWPP.note: Same convention as the existing Assets/Resources/Data/smv/UN-US-*.csv pyramids (verified by the research). Use population / populationWPP to rescale simulated head counts to official totals (0.984 in 2025, 0.982 in 2026).

lifeExpectancy.unit: years (period life expectancy at birth, both sexes)
lifeExpectancy.source: NCHS/CDC: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/cdc_life_exp_raw.csv (1946-1988) and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/life_exp.csv (1989-2023); recalled NCHS final values for 2019-2021 and 2024.
lifeExpectancy.note: 68.2 (1950) -> 78.9 (2014 peak) -> 76.4 (2021, COVID and overdoses) -> 79.0 (2024, record). 2019 (78.8), 2020 (77.0) and 2021 (76.4, final; the mirror shows the provisional 76.1) are recalled NCHS final values; 2024 = 79.0 (NCHS, recalled). Women live ~5 years longer than men (81.1 vs 75.8 in 2023).

totalFertility.unit: children per woman (period total fertility rate)
totalFertility.source: UN WPP 2024 estimates 1950-2023 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PPgp/wpp2024 tfr1dt.rda, research behavior.json totalFertilityRate); 2024 = CDC/NCHS final births data (recalled in the research).
totalFertility.note: Baby-boom peak 3.75 (1958); 1.6 in 2020-2024, a record low 1.599 in 2024 (CDC). UN projections for 2025+ (1.62) are not used; CDC 2025 provisional was not verified. UN estimates run ~0.02-0.03 below CDC in 2019-2021 and within ~0.01 of it in 2022-2023 (CDC ~1.66 and ~1.62), so the 2023 -> 2024 step (UN 1.624 -> CDC 1.599) is not a source artefact.

ageEarningsMale.unit: x = age in years (16..85), NOT a calendar year; v = median earnings at that age / peak-age median (1.0)
ageEarningsMale.source: derived from research history.json personalIncomeByAgeSex_2024_approx (Census PINC-01 shape, recalled), ageEarningsIndex_modeled (Mincer 1974; Murphy & Welch 1990) and activityStatusBySingleAge_2026 (CPS)
ageEarningsMale.note: DERIVED age profile of median earnings, relative to the peak (45-54) = 1.0. Anchors: the research's approximate Census PINC-01 / P-10 median personal income by age and sex for 2024 (history.json personalIncomeByAgeSex_2024_approx, recalled, +/-15%) at group midpoints 29.5 / 39.5 / 49.5 / 59.5 / 69.5 / 80 (+ linear extrapolation to 85), joined by a monotone cubic (PCHIP). Below 29.5 the curve follows the research's Mincer profile exp(0.065x - 0.0012x^2), x = age - 18 (ageEarningsIndex_modeled), raised to the power 1.00 (1 for men; below 1 for women, whose rise from 25 to 45 is flatter in the PINC anchors); below 30 it is multiplied by a logistic student/part-time ramp (scale 3 years, midpoint age 21.7, normalized to 1 at 30) fitted so that age 21 - the median age of employed 15-24 year-olds in CPS activity status 2026 (history.json activityStatusBySingleAge_2026) - sits at the PINC 15-24 ratio (0.24): 16-19 year-olds earn ~5-17% of the peak (part-time, school). CAVEATS: PINC is total income, so 65+ includes Social Security and pensions and the old-age tail is ~0.05-0.1 too high for pure earnings; the research Mincer profile falls faster after 55 (0.65 at 64) than these anchors (0.90 at 55-64). Weighted by the number employed at each age (UN WPP 2025 population x CPS employment share) the profile averages 0.79, so earnings(age) ~ earningsMedian x profile(age) / 0.79 keeps the all-ages level.

ageEarningsFemale.unit: x = age in years (16..85), NOT a calendar year; v = median earnings at that age / peak-age median (1.0)
ageEarningsFemale.source: derived from research history.json personalIncomeByAgeSex_2024_approx (Census PINC-01 shape, recalled), ageEarningsIndex_modeled and activityStatusBySingleAge_2026 (CPS)
ageEarningsFemale.note: DERIVED age profile of median earnings, relative to the peak (45-54) = 1.0. Anchors: the research's approximate Census PINC-01 / P-10 median personal income by age and sex for 2024 (history.json personalIncomeByAgeSex_2024_approx, recalled, +/-15%) at group midpoints 29.5 / 39.5 / 49.5 / 59.5 / 69.5 / 80 (+ linear extrapolation to 85), joined by a monotone cubic (PCHIP). Below 29.5 the curve follows the research's Mincer profile exp(0.065x - 0.0012x^2), x = age - 18 (ageEarningsIndex_modeled), raised to the power 0.54 (1 for men; below 1 for women, whose rise from 25 to 45 is flatter in the PINC anchors); below 30 it is multiplied by a logistic student/part-time ramp (scale 3 years, midpoint age 22.2, normalized to 1 at 30) fitted so that age 21 - the median age of employed 15-24 year-olds in CPS activity status 2026 (history.json activityStatusBySingleAge_2026) - sits at the PINC 15-24 ratio (0.29): 16-19 year-olds earn ~5-17% of the peak (part-time, school). CAVEATS: PINC is total income, so 65+ includes Social Security and pensions and the old-age tail is ~0.05-0.1 too high for pure earnings; the research Mincer profile falls faster after 55 (0.65 at 64) than these anchors (0.90 at 55-64). Weighted by the number employed at each age (UN WPP 2025 population x CPS employment share) the profile averages 0.82, so earnings(age) ~ earningsMedian x profile(age) / 0.82 keeps the all-ages level.

netWorthByAge.unit: x = age of family head in years (midpoint of SCF 2022 age groups), NOT a calendar year; v = median family net worth, 2022 dollars
netWorthByAge.source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances 2022 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Aipinas/capstone-demographic-flows SCF interactive-bulletin mirror; research history.json scfByAgeOfHead_1989_2022)
netWorthByAge.note: Groups: under 35 (x = 28), 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75+ (x = 80). Medians, not means (2022 mean family net worth $1,063,700 vs median $192,900). Wealth peaks at 65-74 and is drawn down slowly after. SCF 2025 results are due late 2026. Use as a calibration target for simulated wealth by age in 2022 (convert with cpi).

homeownershipByAge.unit: x = age of householder in years (midpoint of HVS age groups), NOT a calendar year; v = % of households that own their home (2025)
homeownershipByAge.source: Census HVS Table 19 by age of householder (research behavior.json homeownershipByAge_HVS, recalled +/-1.5 pp) and the HVS total rate (research history.json homeownership_1940_2026)
homeownershipByAge.note: Groups: under 35 (x = 28), 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+ (x = 75). DERIVED for 2025: the research gives 2024 by age (37.4 / 61.9 / 70.8 / 75.6 / 79.0); each is scaled by the change in the total rate (65.28 / 65.62). Under-35 ownership peaked at 43.1% in 2004; the median first-time buyer is now 40 (NAR 2025).

effectiveTaxRate.unit: x = household income percentile (0..100), NOT a calendar year; v = average tax rate, % of income (federal incl. payroll, corporate and excise incidence + state and local)
effectiveTaxRate.source: recalled: CBO "The Distribution of Household Income" (2019-2021 editions, average federal tax rates by income group) + ITEP "Who Pays?" 7th edition (2024, state and local tax rates by income group)
effectiveTaxRate.note: LOW CONFIDENCE (research critique: the CBO figures are recalled and "drive the tax and transfer routing by quintile, so this matters"; +/-3 pp per point). Points at group midpoints: quintiles (10, 30, 50, 70), 81-90 (85), 91-95 (93), 96-99 (97.5), top 1% (99.5); the bottom and top values hold flat beyond. Federal (CBO, pre-pandemic, refundable credits netted): ~0.5 / 8 / 13 / 17 / 19.5 / 21.5 / 24.5 / 31; state and local (ITEP): 11.4 / 10.2 / 9.7 / 9.0 / 8.2 / 8.2 / 7.4 / 7.2 (regressive, sales and property taxes). Denominators differ slightly (CBO: market income + social insurance benefits; ITEP: cash + some noncash income). For the model's personal-tax step (income + payroll taxes only) use the shape and calibrate the level to BEA personal current taxes + contributions ($3,234B + $2,019B in 2025, circuit.json); personalTaxRateCE gives the data-based personal-tax shape.

personalTaxRateCE.unit: x = income percentile (quintile midpoints), NOT a calendar year; v = (personal income taxes + employee payroll taxes) / income before taxes, %
personalTaxRateCE.source: BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024 by income quintile (research spending.json ceSurvey2024ByIncomeQuintile and ceSurvey2024ModelCategoriesByQuintile)
personalTaxRateCE.note: Income before taxes minus income after taxes (federal, state and local income taxes net of refundable credits, so negative for the bottom quintile) plus an estimate of employee Social Security/Medicare deductions (CE all-unit $6,684 spread by wages + 2 x self-employment income, as in spending.json). Excludes employer payroll, sales, property and corporate taxes; CE under-covers the top 1%.

transferShareOfIncome.unit: x = income percentile (quintile midpoints), NOT a calendar year; v = cash transfers / market income, %
transferShareOfIncome.source: BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024 income sources by income quintile (research spending.json ceSurvey2024ByIncomeQuintile)
transferShareOfIncome.note: DERIVED: transfers = 80% of "Social Security, private and government retirement" (assumed Social Security share; national SS benefits $1.45T vs CE-reported retirement income $1.58T, and CE under-reports private pensions) + public assistance / SSI / SNAP + unemployment, workers' comp and veterans' benefits; market income = wages + self-employment + property income + other income + the other 20% (pensions). CASH ONLY: excludes Medicare and Medicaid (~$2.2T in kind) and refundable tax credits, which CBO counts; on the CBO basis the bottom quintile's transfers are roughly twice its market income. Quintiles are ranked by income before taxes, so retirees on Social Security fill the lower quintiles.

savingRateByPercentile.unit: x = household income percentile (quintile midpoints), NOT a calendar year; v = saving, % of disposable income (2024)
savingRateByPercentile.source: BEA Distribution of Personal Income, saving by income quintile 2024 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bdecon/US-chartbook/master/chartbook/data/save_dist.csv; research ownership.json savingByIncomeQuintile_BEA) + BLS CE 2024 after-tax income by quintile (research spending.json) + BEA 2024 personal saving rate, post-Sept-2026 vintage (6.3%)
savingRateByPercentile.note: DERIVED: BEA publishes each quintile's saving only as a % of US median personal income (2024: -38.2 / -10.8 / 19.3 / 67.0 / 191.9); those give each quintile's share of total saving (-0.167 / -0.047 / 0.084 / 0.292 / 0.837). Dividing by each quintile's share of disposable income (CE income after taxes less payroll deductions: 0.041 / 0.098 / 0.157 / 0.243 / 0.461) and multiplying by the national 6.3% gives rates that add up exactly to the national rate. The bottom 40% dissave (retirees drawing down, students, debt, family help); saving is concentrated in the top 40%. UNCERTAIN (+/-5 pp at the ends): CE understates bottom incomes (in-kind benefits), so the bottom rate is probably less negative (~-15% on a CBO income basis); the top quintile average (11%) hides much higher rates for the top 1% (~35% by wealth in circuit.json, after Saez-Zucman). The sibling CE-only rates (spending.json byQuintile: -105% ... +35%) do not add up to the NIPA total.
